statement: A straight path is 20 m long. Trees stand along both sides of it, one every 5 m, with a tree at each end of each side. How many trees are there?

choices.misconception: I divided 20 by 5 and counted only the gaps along one side of the path.
I counted the trees on one side correctly but forgot the other side of the path.
I added a tree at each end to the 4 gaps along one side, counting the end trees twice, and forgot the other side.
I counted the 4 gaps on each side as 4 trees, forgetting that each row has one more tree than gaps.

hints: Draw one side of the path and mark where the trees stand.
A sketch shows that the trees sit at the ends of the gaps, so one row has one more tree than gaps. Then remember the path has two sides.
One side has 20 ÷ 5 = 4 gaps, so 5 trees: at 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20 m. Both sides together have 5 + 5 = 10 trees.

solutions.reliable: Mark one side: trees at 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20 metres, which is 5 trees. The other side is the same, so there are 5 + 5 = 10 trees. The transferable idea: draw a quick sketch to see that a row has one more post than gaps, and to remember every part of the picture.

whyOnTest: A sketch exposes both traps at once: trees outnumber gaps by one, and the path has two sides.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
